strengths: The paper identifies an important limitation of autoregressive camera-guided video generation: it cannot account for future camera poses and may consequently generate geometry that later causes collisions or collapse.

Generative View Stitching is a conceptually simple, training-free extension of diffusion stitching to Diffusion-Forcing video models. Conditioning each target chunk jointly on past and future chunks is practically attractive because it avoids training a specialized backbone.
Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning are clearly motivated, and the paper provides useful ablations separating the effects of stochasticity, guidance, and explicit loop closure.

Across seven designed trajectories and 40 generations, GVS generally improves frame-to-frame consistency, long-range consistency, and the reported collision metric over autoregressive sampling and StochSync. The impossible-staircase example is a compelling demonstration.

The presentation is clear, the algorithm and principal hyperparameters are documented, and the appendix candidly analyzes failures involving external images, wide-baseline viewpoints, and ambiguous trajectories.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow for the paper's broad claims. Only one small, 256x256, eight-frame Diffusion-Forcing backbone trained on RealEstate10K is tested. Thus, compatibility with “any” off-the-shelf Diffusion-Forcing model and relevance to modern video generators are not empirically established.

The benchmark consists of a small set of hand-designed trajectories, with incompletely specified poses and spatial-window construction. Cyclic conditioning appears to require trajectory-specific manual selection of spatial neighbors, limiting the claimed generality and reproducibility of loop closure.

The evidence relies almost entirely on automated proxy metrics. There is no human evaluation of temporal coherence, scene shape-shifting, visual quality, collision avoidance, or loop closure. The collision threshold and spatial-overlap threshold are not specified or validated, and uncertainty or significance statistics are absent despite averaging 40 generations.

Some headline evidence is only qualitative: the 1080-frame stability result is represented by a single example, and the static frame strips cannot substantiate video dynamics well. Camera-trajectory adherence is asserted but not directly quantified.

The baseline coverage is limited to autoregressive sampling and a method originally designed for image synchronization. Comparisons against additional long-video, view-synthesis, or diffusion-composition approaches—and stronger retrieval-based variants—would better establish competitiveness.

The quality trade-off is understated. GVS has substantially worse aesthetic quality than StochSync or autoregressive sampling on some loop trajectories, while the consistency metric can favor oversmoothing. A perceptual study is particularly important here.

Omni Guidance is partly heuristic: Equation 8 merges the two distinct guidance terms from Equation 7 while changing the conditioning removed in the negative branch, but the paper does not derive or carefully justify this approximation beyond empirical results.

No runtime, memory, or scaling comparison is reported, although GVS denoises many windows, uses an extra guidance evaluation, and by default samples the whole sequence jointly. This omission weakens the claim that it is a practical alternative to autoregressive extension. Overall, the idea is promising and technically plausible, but the evidence falls slightly short of top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of autoregressive camera-guided video generation: current frames cannot account for a predefined future trajectory, which can cause collisions and rollout collapse.

GVS is a conceptually simple, training-free adaptation of diffusion stitching to Diffusion-Forcing video models. Jointly denoising target chunks with past and future neighbors is practically appealing.

The comparison uses the same backbone across methods, and the paper includes useful ablations of stochasticity, Omni Guidance, and cyclic loop closing. On the tested trajectories, GVS generally improves frame-to-frame consistency, long-range consistency, and the proposed collision metric.

The paper is clearly organized, provides pseudocode and hyperparameters, and candidly documents important failures involving external image conditioning, wide-baseline viewpoints, and structurally ambiguous trajectories.
The impossible- and indefinite-staircase demonstrations are visually interesting illustrations of the method's potential for long-horizon generation.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow to support the central generality claims. Despite claiming compatibility with any off-the-shelf Diffusion-Forcing video model, experiments use only one low-resolution, 8-frame RE10K backbone. There is no evidence across architectures, training datasets, resolutions, or stronger contemporary video generators.

The benchmark consists of only seven hand-designed camera trajectories, with several variants of essentially the same loop pattern. The loop-closing windows are manually tailored to each trajectory, so the approach is not demonstrated as an automatic solution for arbitrary predefined paths or unknown spatial correspondences.

The derivation of Omni Guidance is insufficiently justified. Equation 7 contains separate unconditional and target-only score terms with coefficients gamma_1 and gamma_2, whereas Equation 8 simply replaces these with one target-only term and a different coefficient. Calling this a merger does not establish that Equation 8 samples from the distribution proposed in Equations 4-6. This weakens the technical foundation of a central claimed contribution.

The reported metrics do not directly establish trajectory fidelity or geometric correctness. Collision avoidance is inferred from monocular video depth and a threshold, while consistency is measured with MEt3R; a method can score well by oversmoothing, suppressing motion, or depicting an incorrect camera transformation. No camera-pose recovery, 3D reconstruction, optical-flow adherence, or human evaluation is provided.

Results report only means over 40 generations, without variances, confidence intervals, paired tests, or per-seed results. Consequently, the reliability of several modest improvements cannot be assessed. The evaluation also omits prompt or scene diversity and reports no systematic failure rate.

Baseline coverage is limited to autoregressive sampling and a repurposed image-stitching method. There are no comparisons with broader long-video, retrieval/memory, view-synthesis, or optimization-based alternatives. Moreover, StochSync uses a substantially different sampling schedule and required adaptation, making it difficult to isolate whether gains arise from the proposed principles or implementation choices.

The headline impossible-staircase result is partly engineered by replacing the disconnected endpoint camera segments with an artificial continuous straight-line segment inside the spatial windows. This is an interesting visual trick, but it weakens the claim that the generated video faithfully follows the supplied camera trajectory.

The method's limitations are central rather than peripheral: it cannot propagate an external initial image, fails on wide-baseline loop closure, and can confuse repeated trajectory structures. These failures substantially restrict controllability and practical camera-guided generation.

No runtime, memory, number-of-model-evaluations, or quality-versus-compute comparison is reported, even though processing many windows throughout denoising is likely much more expensive than autoregressive generation. The 1080-frame result is therefore not convincing evidence of practical scalability.

Overall, the paper presents a promising sampling heuristic with positive results in a controlled setting, but the unresolved derivation issue and limited, method-specific evaluation leave the broad claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper identifies an important limitation of autoregressive camera-guided video generation: it cannot anticipate future camera motion and may therefore generate obstacles that cause later collisions and collapse.

Generative View Stitching is a clear and useful contribution. It repurposes the flexible conditioning interface of Diffusion Forcing models to obtain training-free, bidirectional stitching, avoiding the specialized training required by prior trajectory-stitching methods.

Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning are technically intuitive, practically relevant additions. The ablations separately examine stochasticity, guidance, and explicit loop closure, and support their respective roles.

The evaluation uses a common backbone for all methods, 40 generations per trajectory, several complementary consistency, quality, and collision metrics, and challenging trajectories including long loops and staircases. GVS generally improves substantially over both baselines.

The paper is well written and visually clear, provides detailed pseudocode and hyperparameters, and discusses meaningful failure cases such as external-image propagation, wide-baseline loop closure, and ambiguous trajectory segments.
weaknesses: The empirical scope is narrower than the paper's generality claims. Compatibility with 'any' Diffusion Forcing video model is demonstrated using only one low-resolution, eight-frame-context backbone trained on RealEstate10K; transfer to other architectures, datasets, resolutions, or modern large video models remains unverified.

The benchmark consists of a small collection of manually designed camera trajectories, with only two baselines. StochSync was not designed for temporally coherent video, while the autoregressive baseline is structurally unable to condition on the future, so comparisons against additional long-video, view-synthesis, or optimization-based methods would strengthen the evidence.

The central claims concern video continuity and visual plausibility, but evaluation relies on automated proxy metrics and sparse frame grids. There is no human preference study, statistical uncertainty, or systematic evaluation of camera-pose adherence; collision detection also depends on estimated monocular video depth and a threshold whose sensitivity is not reported.

The derivation of Omni Guidance is more motivational than rigorous. The transition from two guidance terms to the merged heuristic in Eq. 8 is not theoretically justified, and the resulting behavior is supported only empirically on a limited set of settings.

Loop closure requires manually constructed spatial windows based on trajectory-specific correspondences. The Impossible Staircase additionally modifies otherwise disconnected conditioning-camera segments to encourage continuity. These design choices limit automation and weaken the impression of a general loop-closing solution.

Computational cost and scalability are insufficiently quantified. Jointly sampling an entire sequence and making guided model evaluations can be expensive; runtime, memory, number of network evaluations, and quality-versus-compute comparisons with autoregressive sampling are absent.

Important limitations remain substantial: the method cannot reliably propagate an external context image, fails on wide-baseline loops, and may confuse structurally similar trajectory segments. Reproducibility would also benefit from an explicit code-release commitment and complete benchmark assets.

The central idea is technically appealing: GVS reuses the variable-noise conditioning capabilities of Diffusion-Forcing models to perform bidirectional, training-free sequence stitching. Omni Guidance and cyclic conditioning are sensible additions targeting identifiable consistency failures.

The empirical study is substantial: seven trajectories, 40 generations per setting, matched backbone models, multiple consistency and quality metrics, qualitative results, inference-cost measurements, and ablations of guidance, stochasticity, loop closing, sampling steps, chunking, and backbone training schemes.

The reported improvements over autoregressive sampling and StochSync are generally large and consistent, particularly for frame-to-frame consistency and collision avoidance. The authors also investigate a 1080-frame rollout rather than restricting evaluation to short examples.
The limitations section is unusually candid, documenting failures involving external-image propagation, wide-baseline loop closure, online use, and manually specified spatial windows.
weaknesses: The strongest generality claim is insufficiently supported. All three tested backbones share the same 459M U-ViT architecture, RealEstate10K training data, implementation source, resolution, and context length; varying only the diffusion training scheme does not establish compatibility with broadly different off-the-shelf video models.

Loop closing depends on spatial context windows manually designed for each trajectory. These windows supply the relevant long-range correspondences and substantially limit scalability; no automatic construction or evaluation on arbitrary, unseen trajectories is provided.

The baseline set is narrow, consisting principally of autoregressive sampling and an image-stitching method adapted by the authors. Comparisons against stronger noncausal long-video generation, camera-controlled generation, or optimization-based consistency methods would better establish competitiveness.

The evaluation does not directly measure camera-pose adherence. Collision avoidance is inferred through a depth-threshold heuristic, while F2FC can favor static or oversmoothed videos—an issue visible in the authors' own ablations. Frame-quality metrics do not fully resolve this, and no human perceptual study is included.

The paper reports averages without uncertainty intervals or significance tests. Important reproducibility details such as the collision threshold and machine-readable definitions of trajectory-specific spatial windows are missing, and code availability is unclear.

Omni Guidance's transition from the two-scale expression in Eq. 7 to the merged heuristic in Eq. 8 is not rigorously justified. Separate ablations of the camera-guidance and neighbor-consistency terms would clarify which part provides the benefit.

The Impossible Staircase demonstration is highly constructed: the spatial-window camera segments are manually replaced to force visual continuity. It is an interesting illustration, but provides limited evidence for general trajectory-faithful planning.

GVS is a conceptually appealing, training-free adaptation of diffusion stitching, and temporal parallelization offers a useful latency tradeoff relative to autoregressive sampling.
The paper provides substantial ablation coverage, including guidance, stochasticity, loop closing, sampling steps, chunking, inference cost, and three related backbone-training variants.
Experiments average over 40 generations and show consistent improvements over the included baselines in frame consistency, loop consistency, and measured collision avoidance.
The limitations section is unusually candid, documenting failures with external image conditioning, wide-baseline viewpoints, online generation, and scalable neighbor selection.
weaknesses: The central claims are much broader than the evidence. All backbones share the same 459M-parameter architecture, RealEstate10K training data, and source implementation; this does not establish compatibility with arbitrary off-the-shelf Diffusion-Forcing video models or modern large-scale video generators.

Evaluation is confined to seven manually constructed camera trajectories and one narrow indoor-domain model. There is no established benchmark, real-camera evaluation, prompt-conditioned setting, diverse scene/domain study, or human assessment of temporal coherence and visual quality.

Baseline coverage is weak for a top-tier submission: only one autoregressive method and a repurposed image-stitching method are compared. The study omits stronger long-video, camera-control, planning, and 3D-aware alternatives, making it difficult to determine whether the gains come from the proposed ideas or weak comparison points.

Loop closure depends on spatial context windows manually specified for each trajectory. This supplies trajectory-specific structural knowledge and does not scale to arbitrary paths, substantially weakening the claimed general-purpose method.

The evaluation does not directly measure adherence to the requested camera poses or preservation of scene geometry. A depth-threshold collision detector and pairwise feature metrics cannot distinguish correct 3D navigation from smooth deformation, view hallucination, or oversmoothing; the paper itself documents related failures.

Omni Guidance is only partially justified. Equation 7 follows the stated product-of-experts construction, but Equation 8 heuristically merges two distinct guidance terms into a different unconditional masked prediction without a derivation or comparison against the unmerged formulation.

The reported results lack confidence intervals or statistical tests, despite only 40 samples and several modest metric differences. Metric choices and collision thresholds are also insufficiently validated against human judgments.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project-page link is absent, exact trajectory definitions and per-trajectory spatial windows are not provided numerically, and the implementation is promised rather than included in the manuscript.

Overall, the core idea is promising and technically plausible, but the narrow, partially hand-engineered evaluation and unsupported generality claims place the work marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses an important and clearly motivated limitation of autoregressive video generation: inability to account for a predefined future camera trajectory, which can cause collisions and rollout collapse.

Proposes a coherent training-free framework combining parallel diffusion stitching, Omni Guidance, and cyclic conditioning. Compatibility with existing Diffusion-Forcing-style models is practically appealing.

Results across seven challenging trajectories and 40 generations per setting consistently improve frame-to-frame consistency, long-range consistency, and collision avoidance over the evaluated baselines, generally without substantially degrading visual quality.

The evaluation includes useful component, stochasticity, sampling-step, chunking, backbone-training, computational-cost, and long-horizon ablations. The 1080-frame rollout and impossible-staircase demonstration are compelling qualitative applications.

The paper is well organized, visually clear, technically detailed, and unusually candid about limitations such as external-image conditioning, wide-baseline viewpoints, online use, and manual spatial-window construction.
weaknesses: The baseline set is narrow: it contains one autoregressive method and a repurposed image-stitching method. Comparisons with a broader range of long-video, camera-controlled, or optimization-based generation approaches would better establish competitiveness.

External validity is limited. The three backbone variants share the same 459M U-ViT architecture and RealEstate10K training data, while the benchmark consists of a small set of handcrafted trajectories. This does not fully substantiate broad claims about compatibility with off-the-shelf video models.

Cyclic conditioning depends on manually specified, trajectory-specific spatial windows. This materially limits scalability to arbitrary predefined trajectories and makes the strongest loop-closure results rely on additional task knowledge.

Camera-trajectory fidelity is not evaluated directly. Collision detection from estimated depth is only an indirect proxy and cannot establish accurate pose adherence; camera-pose reconstruction error or geometric correspondence metrics would strengthen the central claim.

The quantitative analysis reports means without uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. There is also no human evaluation of temporal coherence, loop closure, or perceptual quality, despite known limitations of the automated metrics.

The transition from the two-term guidance expression in Eq. 7 to the merged approximation in Eq. 8 is only briefly justified, and the ablations do not isolate camera guidance from neighbor-consistency guidance. Reproducibility is also weakened by the missing project-page URL and lack of an explicit code-release artifact in the manuscript.
